cse-2003-cs-70.approach: The loop is Floyd–Warshall with `max` instead of `min`, so entries never decrease and cycles inflate them without bound. Test each option with a 2-cycle, and prove (d) by induction on the largest intermediate vertex.

steps.title: Entries only grow
steps.body: Every update is $A[j,k] \leftarrow \max(A[j,k],\ A[j,i]+A[i,k])$, so each entry is **non-decreasing** over time and always equals the length of *some* walk (not necessarily simple) from $j$ to $k$.

steps.title: A 2-cycle breaks (a), (b), (c)
steps.body:
Take $n=2$, edges $1	o2$, $2	o1$. Trace:

- $i=1$: $A[2,2]=\max(0, A[2,1]+A[1,2]) = 1+1 = 2$.
- $i=2$: $A[1,1]=\max(0, 1+1)=2$; $A[1,2]=\max(1, A[1,2]+A[2,2]) = 1+2 = 3$; $A[2,1]=\max(1, A[2,2]+A[2,1]) = 2+1 = 3$; $A[2,2]=\max(2, 2+2)=4$.

So $A[2,2]=4>n$ — (a) fails. The longest *path* (simple) from 1 to 2 has 1 edge but $A[1,2]=3$ — (c) fails. Add an isolated vertex 3 ($n=3$): still $A[1,1]\ge 2 = n-1$, yet no Hamiltonian cycle exists — (b) fails.

steps.title: Prove (d) by induction
steps.body:
Claim: after iteration $i$, $A[j,k] \ge$ length of every simple $j	o k$ path whose intermediate vertices lie in $\{1,\dots,i\}$.

Take such a path $p$. If it does not use $i$, the claim held earlier and entries never decrease. If it uses $i$, split $p$ at $i$ into simple paths $j\leadsto i$ and $i\leadsto k$ with intermediates in $\{1,\dots,i-1\}$; by induction $A[j,i]\ge|p_1|$ and $A[i,k]\ge|p_2|$, so the update gives $A[j,k]\ge|p_1|+|p_2|=|p|$.

After $i=n$ every simple path is covered, so every simple $j	o k$ path has at most $A[j,k]$ edges.

answer.value: Every simple path from j to k has at most A[j, k] edges

optionAnalysis.reason: False: with a cycle the entries keep growing (2-cycle on n = 2 gives A[2,2] = 4 > 2).
False: A 2-cycle plus an isolated vertex gives A[1,1] ≥ n − 1 with no Hamiltonian cycle.
False: A[j,k] counts lengths of walks that may repeat vertices, so it can exceed the longest simple path (A[1,2] = 3 vs. 1).
True: A[j,k] is an upper bound on every simple path length, proved by induction on the intermediate set {1..i}.

pitfalls: Reading the algorithm as an exact longest-path computer: it computes walk lengths, which overshoot when cycles exist.
Forgetting that entries updated in the same iteration (like A[2,2]) are reused immediately.
cse-2003-cs-70.verification: Hand-traced the 2-cycle example for every entry; the induction argument relies only on monotonicity and the split at the highest-numbered intermediate vertex.

cse-2003-cs-71.approach: Translate each Horn clause: a rule head ← body is a universally quantified implication, and a headless clause ← B is a denial (the body can never hold). Variables appearing only in the body become existential on the left of the implication.

steps.title: The rule
steps.body:
$A(x) \leftarrow B(x,y), C(y)$ means $ orall x\, orall y\,[B(x,y)\wedge C(y) \Rightarrow A(x)]$. Since $y$ does not occur in $A(x)$:

$$ orall y\,[\varphi(y)\Rightarrow A(x)] \equiv [\exists y\,\varphi(y)] \Rightarrow A(x)$$

so the rule is $( orall x)[(\exists y)[B(x,y)\wedge C(y)] \Rightarrow A(x)]$.

steps.title: The goal clause
steps.body: $\leftarrow B(x,x)$ has an empty head, i.e. $\forall x\,[B(x,x)\Rightarrow \text{false}] \equiv \neg(\exists x)[B(x,x)]$.

steps.title: Conjoin
steps.body:
A program is the **conjunction** of its clauses:

$$( orall x)[(\exists y)[B(x,y)\wedge C(y)] \Rightarrow A(x)] \wedge 
eg(\exists x)[B(x,x)]$$

which is option (a).

optionAnalysis.reason: Correct: body-only variable y becomes ∃y on the left of ⇒, and the clauses are conjoined.
Wrong: ∀y inside the antecedent demands B(x,y) ∧ C(y) for every y before concluding A(x) — a much weaker rule.
Wrong: clauses of a program are combined with ∧, not ∨.
Printed identically to (b) in the paper; wrong for the same reason (∀y in the antecedent).

pitfalls: Moving ∀y into the antecedent without flipping it to ∃y.
Treating the headless clause as asserting B(x,x) instead of denying it.
cse-2003-cs-71.verification: Checked the quantifier law ∀y(φ(y) → ψ) ≡ (∃y φ(y)) → ψ when y is not free in ψ.

steps.body:
(a) If $R$ is true, $Q\vee
eg R$ forces $Q$; if $R$ is false, $P\vee R$ forces $P$. Either way $P\vee Q$ holds — resolution is sound.

(b) The consequent contains $R\vee
eg R$, so it is a tautology and the implication is valid.

steps.body: "$(P\vee Q)\Rightarrow\text{FALSE}$" (as a valid statement) says $P\vee Q$ is unsatisfiable, which happens exactly when both $P$ and $Q$ are unsatisfiable.

steps.title: (c) fails

By (a), if $(P\vee R)\wedge(Q\vee
eg R)$ is satisfiable then so is $P\vee Q$. The converse fails: take $P=	ext{true}$, $Q=	ext{false}$, $R=	ext{true}$ (as formulas, e.g. $R = S\vee
eg S$).

- $P\vee Q = 	ext{true}$ — satisfiable.
- $(P\vee R)\wedge(Q\vee
eg R) = 	ext{true}\wedge(	ext{false}\vee	ext{false}) = 	ext{false}$ — unsatisfiable.

So the "if and only if" in (c) is FALSE.

cse-2003-cs-77.approach: CPU utilisation = busy CPU time / length of the steady-state cycle. Simulate one cycle for each policy; whichever stretches the cycle without adding CPU work gives the lowest utilisation.

|---|---|
| Processes | P1, P2 (arrive together) |
| CPU burst | 10 ms |
| I/O burst | 90 ms (parallel) |
| RR quantum | 5 ms |

steps.title: FCFS
steps.body: P1 runs 0–10, P2 runs 10–20. P1's I/O ends at $10+90=100$, P2's at $20+90=110$. Then P1 runs 100–110, P2 110–120, and the pattern repeats every 100 ms.\n\n$$U = \frac{20}{100} = 20\%$$

steps.title: SRTF and static priority
steps.body: Both bursts are equal and the processes never compete (P2 returns from I/O exactly when P1 finishes), so both give the same schedule as FCFS: $U = 20\%$.

steps.title: Round robin, q = 5 ms
steps.body:
P1 0–5, P2 5–10, P1 10–15 (done), P2 15–20 (done). I/O: P1 until $15+90=105$, P2 until $20+90=110$.

P1 105–110, P2 110–115, P1 115–120, P2 120–125; I/O ends at 210 and 215; next CPU activity starts at 210. The cycle is $210-105 = 105$ ms long with 20 ms of CPU work.

$$U =  rac{20}{105} \approx 19.05\%$$

steps.title: Compare
steps.body: Interleaving makes each process finish its burst later (15 and 20 instead of 10 and 20), so the cycle stretches to 105 ms with the same 20 ms of CPU work. $19.05\% < 20\%$, so round robin with a 5 ms quantum gives the least utilisation.

SRTF matches FCFS here (equal bursts, no overlap): 20%.
Static priority also produces the FCFS schedule: 20%.
Correct: the 5 ms quantum delays P1's burst completion, giving a 105 ms cycle: 20/105 ≈ 19%.

steps.body: TLB is always looked up: $1$ ns. On a miss (4%) walk two levels in memory: $2 \times 10 = 20$ ns.\n\n$$T_{\text{trans}} = 1 + 0.04 \times 20 = 1 + 0.8 = 1.8 \text{ ns}$$

steps.title: Data access
steps.body: Cache is checked first: hit costs $1$ ns; miss costs $1 + 10 = 11$ ns.\n\n$$T_{\text{data}} = 0.9 \times 1 + 0.1 \times 11 = 0.9 + 1.1 = 2.0 \text{ ns}$$

Correct: 1.8 + 2.0 = 3.8 ns ≈ 4 ns.

steps.body: Then $(j-1) \mid j$, which forces $j = 2$ — but $j \ge 3$. Not printed.

steps.title: Case j − 1 > T

With $L = \lfloor\log_2 n\rfloor \ge 2$ (i.e. $n\ge4$): $T = 2L$ and $\operatorname{lcm}(1..T) \ge 2^{T-1} = 2^{2L-1} \ge 2^{L+1} > n \ge j$, impossible. Examples: $n=4..7$: $T=4$, lcm $=12 > 7$; $n=8..15$: $T=6$, lcm $=60$. For $n=3$: $T=2$ and $3 \bmod 2 = 1$.

cse-2003-cs-89.approach: Track the global x and P's local x separately; C uses static scoping, so Q sees the global x, and y points to the global x.

steps.title: Enter P
steps.body: Global $x = 5$; \`P(&x)\` sets $y = \&x$. Local \`int x = *y + 2\` $= 5 + 2 = 7$.

steps.title: Q(7)
steps.body: $z = 7$; \`z += x\` uses the **global** $x = 5$: $z = 12$. Prints **12**.

steps.title: Back in P
steps.body: \`*y = x - 1\` uses local $x = 7$: global $x = 6$. \`print(x)\` prints local **7**.

steps.title: main
steps.body: main prints the global x: **6**. Output: 12 7 6.

optionAnalysis.reason: Correct: 7 + 5 = 12, local 7, global 6.
22 12 11 would need P.x = 12 (or global x = 12), which no scoping or passing rule here produces.
14 would use the local x = 7 inside Q (dynamic scoping).
7 would mean Q printed z without adding x.

cse-2003-cs-89.verification: Under dynamic scoping Q would see P's x = 7 and print 14 7 6 (option c) — the C semantics are static, giving 12 7 6.

cse-2003-cs-90.approach: Read the recursion: an empty or one-node list returns 1; otherwise the first two nodes must satisfy data ≤ next data and the rest of the list must satisfy f.

steps.title: Base cases
steps.body: p == NULL or p->next == NULL returns 1: empty and single-element lists are (trivially) sorted.

steps.title: Recursive case
steps.body: Otherwise it returns $(p\to data \le p\to next\to data) \wedge f(p\to next)$. Unrolling: $d_1 \le d_2 \le \dots \le d_m$ — the list is in **non-decreasing** order. Any adjacent pair with $d_i > d_{i+1}$ returns 0.

answer.value: Sorted in non-decreasing order of data

optionAnalysis.reason: Too narrow: e.g. 1 → 2 → 3 also returns 1.
Correct: f checks d_i ≤ d_{i+1} for every adjacent pair.
Reversed comparison: 3 → 2 → 1 returns 0.
A list with all equal values (5 → 5) returns 1, so this is wrong.

cse-2003-cs-90.verification: Tried 1→3→2: 1 ≤ 3 holds, then f(3→2) fails on 3 ≤ 2, returning 0.
